---
title: "Vectors — Directions and Quantities"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

You take three steps east and two north. How do you describe the movement without a story?

## Build the intuition

Use a vector. Its components express how much movement occurs in each independent coordinate direction. Addition combines movements.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
\mathbf u+\mathbf v=(u_1+v_1,\ u_2+v_2)
$$

**Every symbol explained:** u and v are two-dimensional vectors. u₁,v₁ are their horizontal components and u₂,v₂ their vertical components; + adds matching coordinates.

**Substitute real numbers:** If u=(3,2) and v=(−1,4), add horizontal parts 3+(−1)=2 and vertical parts 2+4=6; the sum is (2,6).

## Why the relationship is true

Following one displacement then another gives the same net displacement as adding their coordinate components. This is the geometric vector-addition rule.

## Where the shortcut stops working

A vector is not the same as a point, even though both may be written with two numbers; a point is a location, a displacement is a difference between locations.

## Your turn

Compute (3,2)−(−1,4), then explain the movement in everyday words.

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Intro to linear algebra, §§2.1–2.2. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
